## What every acoustic measure sees

Every acoustic measure in this reference is computed on a digital signal —
a sequence of numeric samples that represents the microphone's continuous
pressure waveform. The chain from a spoken vowel to a jitter value passes
through five stages this chapter defines:

1. **Sampling** — picking amplitude at regularly spaced time points.
2. **Quantization** — mapping continuous amplitude to a finite set of levels.
3. **Framing** — cutting the sample stream into short segments for
   time-varying analysis.
4. **Windowing** — tapering each frame to control spectral artefacts.
5. **Spectral or cepstral transformation** — moving from the time domain
   into a domain where harmonic structure and periodicity are visible.

Each stage introduces choices (sampling rate, bit depth, frame length,
window shape, transform length) that constrain what a downstream measure
can and cannot say. Every measure chapter in Parts II–IV names the specific
frame length and window it presupposes; this chapter is the reference those
cross-references resolve to.

## Signals: continuous and discrete

An **analog signal** varies continuously in both time and amplitude — the
voltage produced by a microphone as a vowel is spoken. A **digital signal**
is discrete in both dimensions: time is discretized by sampling, amplitude
by quantization [@ludlow2018measuring]. The transformation from continuous
to digital is analog-to-digital conversion (A/D); the reverse — needed to
play a sample stream through a loudspeaker — is D/A conversion
[@kent2002acoustic].

The digital sequence *x*[*n*] represents the analog signal *x*(*t*) at
instants *t* = *nT*, where *T* is the sampling period. What was a function
of continuous time becomes a numbered sequence.

## Sampling and Nyquist

The **sampling rate** is the number of samples per second, in hertz. A
sampling rate of 10 kHz means the analog signal is sampled 10,000 times
per second [@kent2002acoustic].

**Nyquist's Sampling Theorem** states that the sampling rate must be at
least twice the highest frequency of interest in the signal
[@kent2002acoustic; @rabiner2011theory]. For voice analysis this fixes the
practical minimum:

| Sampling rate | Maximum analysable frequency |
|---|---|
| 44.1 kHz (CD quality) | 22.05 kHz |
| 22.05 kHz | 11.025 kHz |
| 10 kHz | 5 kHz |
| 8 kHz (telephone) | 4 kHz |

Sampling below the Nyquist rate produces **aliasing** — high-frequency
energy folds down into the analysis band and misrepresents the signal.
Aliasing is prevented by a **pre-sampling (anti-alias) low-pass filter**
placed before the sampler, rejecting energy above the Nyquist frequency. A
useful filter target for speech work is at most 0.5 dB pass-band ripple and
at least −68 dB stop-band attenuation [@kent2002acoustic].

## Quantization

Quantization discretizes amplitude. Instead of a continuous voltage, each
sample is represented by an integer drawn from 2^*N* levels, where *N* is
the **bit depth** [@ludlow2018measuring]:

| Bit depth | Levels |
|---|---|
| 8 | 256 |
| 10 | 1,024 |
| 12 | 4,096 |
| 16 | 65,536 |
| 24 | 16,777,216 |

The greater the bit depth, the finer the amplitude gradation and the
smaller the quantization error. For voice measurement, 16 bits (a
signal-to-quantization-noise ratio around 96 dB) is the practical standard;
@baken2000clinical treat 10 bits as a defensible minimum, and note that
using as much of the converter's input range as possible is at least as
important as high bit depth, because quantization error is a fixed absolute
quantity — a small signal wastes bit depth.

Set the input gain conservatively (peak at ~80 % of full scale) and check
for clipping in every recording. A clipped signal distorts every derived
measure — F0, jitter, shimmer, HNR, CPP.

## Framing and windowing

Voice signals are non-stationary — the vocal-tract configuration and
glottal source change from vowel to vowel and even within a single vowel.
A single global Fourier transform of a long utterance therefore averages
away most of what matters. **Short-time analysis** solves this by dividing
the signal into overlapping short segments (**frames**) and analysing each
frame as if it were locally stationary [@rabiner2011theory].

- **Frame length** is typically 20–40 ms for voice analysis: long enough to
  contain several pitch periods, short enough that the vocal-tract
  configuration doesn't change appreciably across the frame.
- **Frame rate** (or hop size) is how often frames are extracted, typically
  every 5–10 ms. Frames overlap by 50–75 %.
- **Windowing** multiplies each frame by a tapered function before the
  Fourier transform, to suppress the spectral artefacts that a rectangular
  frame would produce.

The **Hamming window** is the standard choice for voice work:

$$
w[n] = 0.54 - 0.46 \cos\!\left(\frac{2\pi n}{N-1}\right), \quad 0 \le n \le N-1
$$

[@rabiner2011theory]. It suppresses the side lobes of a rectangular window
at the cost of a slightly wider main lobe (worse frequency resolution). The
**Hanning (Hann) window**, a related raised-cosine variant, is used
equivalently in many systems. The rectangular window — no tapering — is
used only when frame boundaries coincide with signal periods (rare in
practice).

The trade-off between frame length and frequency resolution is fixed by an
uncertainty-like relation Δ*f* ≈ 1/*T*: a longer frame *T* gives finer
frequency resolution Δ*f*, but averages over more temporal change. A 30-ms
Hamming window at a 44.1 kHz sampling rate gives about 33 Hz frequency
resolution, which is finer than a semitone at typical speaking F0.

## Time, frequency, and cepstral domains

Three domains carry voice information, and different measures live in
different domains:

**Time domain.** The sample sequence *x*[*n*]. Waveform-based measures
(jitter, shimmer, autocorrelation-based F0 trackers) work here.

**Frequency domain (spectrum).** Obtained by applying a discrete Fourier
transform (DFT, computed as an FFT) to a windowed frame. Magnitude gives
the short-time magnitude spectrum; a series of such spectra across time is
a spectrogram. Harmonics-to-noise ratio, spectral tilt, and formant
measurements live here.

**Cepstral domain (cepstrum).** Obtained by taking the logarithm of the
magnitude spectrum and applying an inverse Fourier transform to it
[@rabiner2011theory]. Its independent variable is **quefrency** — a
time-like dimension in units of seconds — and its dominant peak sits at
the quefrency corresponding to the voice period. The cepstrum is where
cepstral peak prominence lives; see the [CPPS chapter](cpps.qmd).

The mathematical definition of periodicity — *f*(*t* + *T*) = *f*(*t*),
where *T* is the period — is what all of this ultimately measures against
[@titze2000principles]. When the periodicity condition fails, so do most
of these measures; see the [Signal Typing chapter](foundations-signal-typing.qmd).

## Caveats

- **Sampling rate and analysis bandwidth are not the same as the highest
  recovered frequency.** A 44.1 kHz recording preserves energy up to 22 kHz
  in principle, but only if the anti-alias filter actually rejects energy
  above the Nyquist frequency to that fidelity.
- **Frame length gates what can be measured.** A frame shorter than one
  voice period cannot support F0 or perturbation measurement. For a
  speaker at 100 Hz (10 ms per period), a 20 ms frame contains two
  periods — the minimum defensible for jitter or shimmer, well below the
  ≥30-cycle sample @baken2000clinical recommend for shimmer.
- **Window choice affects spectral tilt and formant measurements.** A
  Hamming window's main-lobe width is roughly 8π/*N* radians on a length-*N*
  frame; comparing measurements across studies requires the same window
  family and length.
- **Software defaults differ.** Praat, ADSV, MDVP, and PhonaLab each ship
  with different default frame lengths, hop sizes, windows, and
  pre-emphasis coefficients. Every reported measure in this reference
  names its software and settings; a bare number without them is not
  comparable across systems.
- **Digitisation is not lossless.** The finite sampling rate and bit depth
  set floors on what any downstream measure can resolve. Perturbation
  measures are especially sensitive to quantization noise at low bit
  depth [@baken2000clinical].
